facts.statement: Fossils of Cladoselache were discovered in the Cleveland Shale on the south shore of Lake Erie.
facts.quote: discovered in the Cleveland Shale on the south shore of Lake Erie.

facts.statement: Cladoselache had a body shape similar to modern lamnid sharks like mako and great white sharks, but was not closely related to them.
facts.quote: It was similar in body shape to modern lamnid sharks (such as mako sharks and the great white shark), but was not closely related to lamnids or to any other modern (selachian) shark.

facts.statement: Cladoselache grew to several meters in length and was likely a fast-moving, agile marine predator with a streamlined body and deeply forked tail.
facts.quote: Growing to several meters in length, Cladoselache is considered to have been a fast-moving and fairly agile marine predator due to its streamlined body and deeply forked tail.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Cladoselache had at least five pairs of slender, well-separated branchial arches, resulting in five gill slits on each side of its body.
facts.quote: The gill basket is poorly known, but available evidence points towards the presence of at least five pairs of slender and well-separated branchial arches, and therefore five gill slits on either side of the body.

facts.statement: Cladoselache's tail was tapered and keeled, ending in a crescent-shaped caudal fin.
facts.quote: The caudal peduncle (tail) is tapered and keeled, ending at a crescent-shaped caudal fin.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest Cladoselache is closely related to symmoriiforms based on distinctive traits of its chondrocranium, dorsal fin spines, and pectoral fin bases.
facts.quote: More recent studies have identified distinctive traits of the chondrocranium (cartilaginous braincase), dorsal fin spines, and pectoral fin bases. These newly identified features support a close relationship to symmoriiforms, a small group of bizarre chondrichthyans such as the bristle-spined Stethacanthus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Cladoselache and symmoriiforms are more closely related to chimaeras than to true sharks and rays.
facts.quote: Cladoselache and symmoriiforms may be more closely related to chimaeras (a modern group of unusual deep-sea fish) than to true sharks and rays.

facts.statement: Early sources suggested Cladoselache might have had six or seven gill slits, but this has not been confirmed.
facts.quote: Some early sources have suggested that six or even seven gill slits may have been present, though this has not been confirmed.

facts.statement: All fins of Cladoselache except the tail fin had a wide base continuous with the torso and were supported by cartilaginous rods called radials.
facts.quote: All of the fins (except the caudal fin) have the same basic structure: a wide base which is continuous with the torso, and a subtriangular profile supported along nearly the whole length of the fin by cartilaginous rods known as radials.

facts.statement: Cladoselache possessed a large, elongated pectoral fin connected to a strong and broad girdle.
facts.quote: The pectoral fin is large and elongated, connecting to a strong and broad pectoral girdle.

facts.statement: No claspers have ever been found in Cladoselache fossils.
facts.quote: Claspers have never been found in Cladoselache, despite their presence in close relatives and even other Devonian chondrichthyans.

facts.statement: Cladoselache appears to have lacked an anal fin.
facts.quote: Cladoselache appears to lack an anal fin.

facts.statement: Cladoselache had a distinctive tall, crescent-shaped tail fin extending from a narrow base.
facts.quote: The caudal fin is distinctive, with a very tall and lunate (crescent moon-shaped) profile extending from a narrow tail base.

facts.statement: Cladoselache had two dorsal fins, with the first located above the pectoral fins and being significantly taller than the second.
facts.quote: There are two dorsal fins: the first dorsal fin is located above the pectoral fins and is significantly taller than the second dorsal fin, which is located above the pelvic fins.

facts.statement: A stout spine-like structure was found in front of the first dorsal fin of Cladoselache in specimens described in 1938.
facts.quote: However, a stout spine-like structure is now known to have been present in front of the first dorsal fin, according to specimens which were first described in 1938.

facts.statement: Cladoselache is considered an early member of the Chondrichthyes, the group of cartilaginous fish.
facts.quote: Cladoselache is considered one of the best-known early members of the Chondrichthyes: cartilaginous fish such as sharks, rays, and the deep-sea chimaeras (also known as ratfish or ghostsharks).

facts.statement: Cladoselache is not a member of the modern shark group (Selachii), which evolved later in the Jurassic Period.
facts.quote: Though it resembles modern sharks (selachians) in ecology and body shape, it is not a member of that group, which did not evolve until the Jurassic Period.

facts.statement: Cladoselache is often described as a basal chondrichthyan rather than a true shark.
facts.quote: It and other Paleozoic "sharks" may instead be described as basal chondrichthyans, a term indicating their origin at an earlier stage in cartilaginous fish evolution.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding whether Cladoselache was the earliest-diverging member of Chondrichthyes or an elasmobranch that originated after holocephalans.
facts.quote: Some studies argued that it was the earliest-diverging member of the group, while others placed it as an elasmobranch, originating slightly later than the holocephalans.

facts.statement: Some studies suggested Cladoselache was a derived elasmobranch close to hybodonts and modern sharks, but this view was considered uncertain and unstable.
facts.quote: A few studies even suggested that it was a more derived elasmobranch close to hybodonts and neoselachians (modern sharks and rays), though this was an uncertain and unstable position.

facts.statement: Cladoselache may belong to an early-diverging clade at the base of Chondrichthyes or Elasmobranchii alongside symmoriiforms.
facts.quote: Symmoriiforms and Cladoselache may form an early-diverging clade at the base of Chondrichthyes or Elasmobranchii

facts.statement: An alternative hypothesis suggests Cladoselache lies on the holocephalan stem-group leading to modern chimaeras.
facts.quote: Symmoriiforms (including Cladoselache) may lie on the opposite side of Chondrichthyes, as an early part of the holocephalan stem-group which would eventually produce modern chimaeras

facts.statement: Cladoselache had slender, smooth-edged teeth adapted for grasping prey rather than tearing or chewing.
facts.quote: The teeth of Cladoselache were slender and smooth-edged, making them suitable for grasping, but not tearing or chewing

facts.statement: Stomach contents preserved in Cladoselache fossils indicate it was a predator that ate small ray-finned fishes, thylacocephalan arthropods, conodonts, and hagfish-like proto-vertebrates.
facts.quote: Within the gut of most Cladoselache fossils were remnants of their stomach contents

facts.statement: The presence of fish remains found tail-first in Cladoselache stomachs suggests it was a fast and agile hunter.
facts.quote: Some of the fish remains were found tail first within the stomach, indicating that Cladoselache was a fast and agile hunter

facts.statement: The method of reproduction in Cladoselache remains unresolved, as it lacks known claspers despite other early shark fossils showing them.
facts.quote: A mystery that has yet to be resolved is its method of reproduction

facts.statement: Cladoselache possessed tiny, bluntly conical placoid scales that were absent from much of its body.
facts.quote: Placoid scales (denticles) were present in Cladoselache, but they are tiny and bluntly conical structures which are absent from much of the body

facts.statement: The eyes of Cladoselache were protected by a ring of more than 20 small dermal ossifications.
facts.quote: The eye was protected by a ring of numerous (more than 20) small dermal ossifications

facts.statement: The musculature of Cladoselache consisted of discrete packages of muscle fibers that were easier to differentiate than in modern sharks.
facts.quote: The musculature of Cladoselache is organized into discrete packages of muscle fibers, which are easier to differentiate than those of modern sharks

facts.statement: Unlike modern sharks, Cladoselache's skin was not entirely covered in dermal denticles, possessing them only around the fins and eyes.
